title: LLM Pretraining and Adaptation
description: How large language models are trained, adapted, and evaluated.

questions.prompt: What is the standard next-token objective for a causal language model?
options: Predict the next token from preceding context
Reconstruct each input pixel
Classify every token by sentiment
Sort tokens by frequency
questions.explanation: The model is trained to assign high probability to the observed next token given its prior context.

questions.prompt: Why can a token count differ substantially from a word count?
options: Tokenizers split text into subword units and symbols
Every word always maps to two tokens
Tokens count only punctuation
A token is a sentence by definition
questions.explanation: A tokenizer may represent a word as one or several tokens; punctuation and whitespace patterns also affect tokenization.

questions.prompt: A pretrained language model’s behavior can be influenced by patterns and omissions in its training corpus.
questions.explanation: Training data shapes learned associations, including useful information and potential biases or gaps.

questions.prompt: What is a context window?
options: The maximum amount of token context a model can process in one input
A window in a user interface
The number of optimizer steps
The count of training documents
questions.explanation: Context length limits how many tokens the model can condition on in a given inference pass.

questions.prompt: What can continued pretraining on domain text do?
options: Adapt language patterns toward that domain
Guarantee factual correctness
Expose the model to additional domain vocabulary
Replace downstream evaluation
questions.explanation: Continued pretraining can improve domain familiarity, but does not guarantee factuality or remove the need for evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is instruction tuning intended to teach a language model?
options: Respond to natural-language task instructions
Use a different tokenizer for every prompt
Memorize the evaluation labels
Always decline uncertain questions
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning trains on instruction-response examples to improve task following.

questions.prompt: What does preference-based optimization use as a training signal?
options: Comparisons or rankings of candidate responses
Only token frequencies from a corpus
A list of model file sizes
Unlabeled image dimensions
questions.explanation: Preference methods use judgments about which outputs are preferred, directly or through a learned reward model.

questions.prompt: A reward model trained from human preferences is itself guaranteed to capture every user’s values.
questions.explanation: Preference data reflects particular annotators and instructions, and its learned reward can be incomplete or misaligned.

questions.prompt: What does perplexity measure for a language model on a text sequence?
options: Exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token
The number of parameters in a checkpoint
The number of generated paragraphs
The average response length in words
questions.explanation: Perplexity summarizes predictive likelihood, but tokenization and dataset differences affect comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which practices improve interpretation of an LLM evaluation?
options: Use task-relevant examples
Report the prompt and evaluation setup
Inspect errors and subgroup behavior
Treat one benchmark score as a universal guarantee
questions.explanation: Evaluation context and error analysis matter; a single benchmark cannot establish universal capability.

questions.prompt: In few-shot prompting, what does the prompt contain?
options: A small number of example input-output demonstrations
A full parameter update for each query
Only the model’s vocabulary
A replacement training corpus
questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting provides demonstrations in context without necessarily updating model weights.

questions.prompt: In-context learning generally changes a language model’s stored parameters for every new prompt.
questions.explanation: The model conditions on prompt examples at inference; its parameters usually remain fixed.

questions.prompt: What does increasing sampling temperature generally do?
options: Flatten the next-token distribution and increase randomness
Reduce context length
Change the tokenizer vocabulary
Make all tokens equally likely
questions.explanation: Temperature rescales logits before sampling; higher values usually make lower-ranked alternatives more likely.

questions.prompt: Which are decoding strategies or controls?
options: Top-k sampling
Nucleus (top-p) sampling
Beam search
Gradient descent on user input during ordinary generation
questions.explanation: Top-k, top-p, and beam search control sequence selection; gradient descent is not ordinary decoding.

questions.prompt: What is a common limitation of beam search in open-ended text generation?
options: It can favor generic outputs and does not guarantee human preference
It samples uniformly from all possible texts
It requires training a new tokenizer
It always returns the globally most factual response
questions.explanation: Beam search optimizes a sequence score and may produce bland outputs; likelihood is not the same as quality.

questions.prompt: Fine-tuning examples can introduce new behaviors and failure modes as well as improve task performance.
questions.explanation: The adaptation dataset and objective can shift model behavior, so outcomes require evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is catastrophic forgetting during model adaptation?
options: Previously learned capabilities degrade while learning new data
The model forgets how to tokenize any word
A hard drive deletes the checkpoint
A prompt exceeds the context window
questions.explanation: Strong adaptation to new data can overwrite or degrade capabilities learned earlier.

questions.prompt: Which are parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches?
options: Low-rank adapters
Adapter modules
Updating a small subset of parameters
Retraining every base parameter as a requirement
questions.explanation: PEFT updates small added or selected parameter sets rather than requiring full-model training.

questions.prompt: What is benchmark data contamination?
options: Evaluation examples or answers appeared in training data
The prompt includes a typo
The model uses a large vocabulary
The benchmark has more than one metric
questions.explanation: Contamination can inflate scores because the model may have seen benchmark content during training.

questions.prompt: Why can prompting style affect an LLM capability evaluation?
options: A task may require instructions or formats that elicit the capability
The model’s parameter count changes with wording
The tokenizer always changes randomly
Prompt wording alters the ground truth
questions.explanation: Poorly matched prompts can fail to elicit a capability, so evaluation protocols should be explicit and robust.
